title: Both At Once.
author: Chris O'Brien
summary: A school-leadership writer dismantles the popular claim that teacher-student relationships alone drive better student behavior, arguing that "feeling cared about does not produce better executive functioning any more than it produces the ability to divide fractions." Drawing on Judith Kleinfeld's 1975 warm-demander research and Lisa Delpit's later popularization of the term, he lays out a five-part behavioral definition of the warm demander — seeing the student accurately, being credible, being predictable, holding an unmovable standard, and telling the truth with a next step attached — applied consistently regardless of how the student behaves on a given day. His sharper point is diagnostic: advising teachers to simply "build the relationship" is corrosive because its success condition is a feeling inside someone else's head, which can never be confirmed and can always be pursued further, producing an unbounded standard that burns teachers out rather than an achievable one. He closes with a surgeon analogy — bedside manner earns trust but teaches nothing about operating — to argue that behavioral self-regulation is a separate teachable discipline from relationship-building, one schools have spent thirty years failing to hand teachers as its own body of knowledge.
points: Kleinfeld's 1975 study crossed warmth against demandingness to identify four teacher types — Sophisticates, Traditionalists, Sentimentalists, and Warm Demanders — and found only the warm-and-demanding combination effective with the students she studied.

"Working on the relationship" is corrosive advice for teachers because its success condition is a feeling inside another person's head: it can never be confirmed, can always be pursued further, and therefore produces an unbounded standard that leads to exhaustion rather than excellence.

Per Hattie, teacher credibility is one of the strongest predictors of student learning — stronger than student effort, motivation, or socioeconomic status — which reframes "knowing your content" as a relational asset, not just an academic one.
High expectations are defined operationally, not as a belief: "they're a record of refusals" — you may scaffold the support up, but the work itself, and the standard it must meet, never moves down.

Behavioral self-regulation is a separate, teachable discipline from relationship-building — like a surgeon's bedside manner, the relationship earns trust and cooperation but teaches the child nothing about how to actually regulate, start tasks, or recover from embarrassment.
quotes: Feeling cared about does not produce better executive functioning any more than it produces the ability to divide fractions.

She found teachers varied along two dimensions rather than one. The first ran from personal warmth to professional distance. The second ran from active demandingness to passive leniency. Cross them and you get four teachers.
High expectations aren't a belief, they're a record of refusals. You may scaffold up, but you never water down.

Its success condition is a feeling inside another person's head. You can't see it, you can't confirm it, and you can always care more, so there is no version of done. A conscientious teacher works until she's empty and still has no evidence she succeeded.
That isn't a high standard. It's an unbounded one, and unbounded standards don't produce excellence. They produce exhaustion, then resentment.

Think about a surgeon. Bedside manner determines whether a patient trusts her, follows instructions, tells the truth about his symptoms, comes back for the follow-up. It is not optional and it is not soft. It also teaches her nothing about how to operate, and none of us would accept a surgeon who had only studied the first one.

We told teachers the relationship was the whole practice, never gave them the other half, and then when a child's behavior didn't improve, sent them back to the half we'd given them and told them to do more of it.
